items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S8065

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the economic development law and the public authorities
law, in relation to the creation of the energize New York power program;
and to amend the economic development law, the public authorities law,
the tax law, chapter 316 of the laws of 1997 amending the public author-
ities law and other laws relating to the provision of low cost power to
foster statewide economic development, and chapter 645 of the laws of
2006 amending the economic development law and other laws relating to
reauthorizing the New York power authority to make contributions to the
general fund, in relation to extending the expiration of the power for
jobs program and the energy cost savings benefit program; and to repeal
subdivision 16 of section 1005 of the public authorities law relating to
energy audits

PURPOSE:

This bill would create a new permanent, 910 megawatt (MW), Energize New
York Power Program administered by the Power Authority of the State of
New York (NYPA) and the Economic Development Power Allocation Board
(EDPAB) to foster job creation and retention in New York State. The new
program would consist of a combination of NYPA hydropower and competi-
tively purchased market power for allocation to eligible businesses and
other entities located in the State. To accomplish this important objec-
tive, the bill would reallocate up to 455 MW of hydroelectric power
currently used by certain domestic and rural consumers, and extend for
one year and then phase out the existing Power for Jobs (PFJ) and Energy
Cost Savings Benefit (ECSB) programs. In addition, the bill would
provide for financial assistance and energy efficiency measures to help
mitigate effects on domestic and rural consumers resulting from the
reallocation of hydropower that would be used to support the new Ener-
gize New York Power Program.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill would provide the short title of the bill as the
"Energize New York Power Program Act."

Section 2 of the bill would add a new section 188-a to the Economic
Development Law (EDL) to create the Energize New York Power Program.
Section 188-a would, among other things:

* Define terms used in EDL § 188-a.

* Authorize EDPAB to solicit applications for the new Energize New York
Power Program (ENYPP) beginning January 31, 2011, and make recommenda-
tions to NYPA for allocations under ENYPP beginning July 1, 2011.

* Establish eligibility for ENYPP allocations and provide limitations on
who may receive allocations under ENYPP.

* Establish notice requirements for applications for ENYPP power allo-
cations.

* Establish criteria for an ENYPP allocation award, which would be
considered in the aggregate and include the following:

* significance of electricity costs to the applicant;
* extent to which an award of power to the applicant will result in
new capital investments in the State;
* extent to which an allocation of power is consistent with state,
local and regional economic development strategies and priorities;
* types of facilities the applicant proposes to construct, enlarge or
install as consideration for an ENYPP allocation;
* applicant's payroll;
* number of jobs the applicant would create or retain in relation to
the size of the ENYPP power allocation requested;
* risk that the applicant would leave the State, curtail operations or
lose jobs without an ENYPP allocation;
* significance of the applicant's facilities to the local economy;
* extent to which the applicant has invested in energy efficiency
measures, will agree to make tangible investments in energy
efficiency measures, or will agree to participate in energy audits of
its facilities;
* consistency between the applicant's operations and the policies and
goals of the State energy plan;
* whether the applicant receives benefits under other NYPA programs;
* extent to which a power allocation might result in an advantage as
compared to its competitors in the State; and
* regarding
not-for-profit corporation applicants, the extent to which the
applicant provides critical services or substantial benefits to the
local community.

* Establish an initial term of up to 7 years for ENYPP allocations and
contracts, and authorize extensions of allocations and contracts.

* Authorize EDPAB to recommend reductions of ENYPP allocations at
facilities if actual metered load is less than the allocation and
reallocate relinquished or withdrawn ENYPP allocations consistent
with the provisions contained therein.

* Authorize EDPAB and NYPA to require applicants to agree to
periodic audits to ensure compliance with contract terms and ENYPP
requirements.

* Provide that EDPAB: (1) shall not allocate more than 910 MW of ENYPP
allocations; (2) shall set aside at least 320 MW of ENYPP allocations
for use at facilities located within the National Grid, New York
State Electric and Gas (NYSEG), and Rochester Gas and Electric

(RG&E) service territories; (3) shall set aside up to 100 MW of ENYPP
allocations for eligible small businesses and not-for-profit
corporations; and (4) shall set aside at least 200 MW of ENYPP
allocation for the purposes of attracting new business to New York,
encouraging new capital investment in New York and creating new jobs
in New York.

* Authorize EDPAB to choose between eligible applicants based on
which applicants best meet applicable criteria, require EDPAB to
issue recommendations on applications in writing, and provide that a
recommendation for an ENYPP allocation qualifies the applicant to
enter into a contract with NYPA on appropriate terms and conditions.

* Provide for the partial and complete withdrawal of power from ENYPP
participants for non-compliance with agreed-upon commitments.

* Require NYPA and the Department of Public Service (DPS) to make
recommendations to the Public service Commission (PSC) for reduced
rates applicable to the delivery by utility corporations of ENYPP
allocations, and provide that any such recommendation for reduced
delivery rates would be at such level as to allow the utility to (i)
recover the incremental cost of providing delivery service to such
customers, and (ii) contribute to the common delivery and related
costs which otherwise would be borne by other customers.

* Restrict the transfer of ENYPP allocations and contracts.

Require the EDPAB, in consultation with NYPA, to report on the
effectiveness of the ENYPP.

Section 3 of the bill would add a new subdivision 13-a to Public
Authorities Law (PAL) § 1005 to authorize NYPA to make ENYPP
allocations and enter into contracts to sell up to 910 MW to eligible
applicants upon recommendation of EDPAB. This new subdivision would
also provide that power used in ENYPP will consist of: (1) up to 455
MW of hydroelectricity withdrawn as of June 1, 2010 from utility
corporations to which it was allocated for the benefit of these
companies' domestic and rural consumers (residential consumers); and
(2) up to an equal amount of market power. ENYPP allocations would
consist of equal parts of NYPA hydropower and market power and would
be sold to all eligible applicants on a uniform basis.

Subdivision 13-a would further provide that NYPA, prior to entering
into a contract with eligible applicants for the sale of ENYPP power,
and prior to the provision of electric service relating to an
ENYPP allocation, shall offer eligible applicants the option to decline
to purchase the market power component of such ENYPP allocation.
If an applicant declines to purchase the market power component through
ENYPP, the applicant would  be responsible for acquiring any
such power on its own behalf.

Section 4 of the bill would add a new subdivision 13-b to PAL § 1005
to authorize NYPA to implement two residential consumer discount
programs to help mitigate the cost impacts on residential customers
resulting from the reallocation of hydroelectricity for use in the
ENYPP. Under a new "Residential Consumer Electricity Cost Discount"
program, NYPA would be authorized, as deemed feasible and advisable
by the Trustees, to fund monthly payments to be made to such classes
of electricity consumers, as enjoyed the benefits of authority
hydroelectric power withdrawn pursuant to subdivision 13-a of PAL
1005. The monthly payments would commence after the hydroelectric
power is withdrawn and the total annual amount of the temporary
monthly payments for the first 12-month period following the
withdrawal would be $100 million. The total annual amount of
temporary monthly payments for the five subsequent 12-month periods
would decline by $14 million from each prior year. Thereafter, the
total amount of monthly payments for each 12 month period would be
$30 million. Beginning with the second year of the Residential
Consumer Electricity Cost Discount program, up to $8 million annually
would be set aside for an "Agricultural Consumer Electricity
Cost Discount" program to provide supplemental discounts to
agricultural producers who receive electric service at the
residential rate. The PSC would supervise the distribution of this
funding through jurisdictional utility rates, according to the
relative amounts of hydropower purchased by the utilities.

Section 5 of the bill would add a new subdivision 18 to PAL § 1005 to
require NYPA to complete detailed annual reports on each economic
development power program it administers.

Section 6 of the bill would provide that, with respect to applicants
who are in substantial compliance with contractual commitments and
receiving benefits under the existing Power for Jobs, Energy Cost
Savings Benefit, Economic Development, High Load Factor or Municipal
Distribution Agency programs, but who would otherwise not receive a
recommendation from the EDPAB for an ENYPP allocation, the EDPAB
shall recommend that NYPA provide for a "transitional electricity
discount." Such applicants may receive payments from NYPA as
follows: (1) in the year beginning July 1, 2011 and in the year
beginning July , 2012, in an amount equal to 66% of the benefits
they received under the expiring programs during the 12 months ending
May 15, 2010; and (2) in the year beginning July 1, 2013 and in the
year beginning July 1, 2014, in an amount equal to 33% of such
benefits. The Transitional Electricity Discount payments would end
June 30, 2015.

Section 7 of the bill would amend § 9 (the effective date section) of
Chapter 316 of the Laws of 1997 to extend the current June 2, 2010
sunset of the Chapter to June 30, 2011. The Chapter, among other
things, created the PFJ program in EDL § 189.

Section 8 of the bill would amend § 11 (the effective date section) of
Chapter 645 of the Laws of 2006 to extend the current June 2, 2010

sunset of § 7 of that Chapter to June 30, 2011. Section 7 of the
Chapter provides for certain responsibilities of NYPA, the Director
of the Budget and the Comptroller relating to the PFJ program.

Section 9 of the bill would amend EDL § 183(h)(2) and (4) to extend
the current June 2, 2010 sunset of the ESCB program to June 30, 2011.

Section 10 of the bill would amend the opening paragraph of paragraph
5 of EDL § 189(a) to extend the current June 2, 2010 sunset of the PFJ
Electricity Savings Reimbursements to June'30, 2011 at the same level
as provided under such program during the 12 months ending May 15, 2010.

Section 11 of the bill would amend EDL § 189(f) and (1) to provide for
the extension of Power for Jobs contracts and rebates through June
30, 2011.

Section 12 of the bill would amend Tax Law § 186(9) to extend the
taxable periods for which a utility that delivers PFJ power is
allowed a tax credit through 2011.

Section 13 of the bill would amend subparagraph 2 of paragraph (g) of
the ninth undesignated paragraph of PAL § 1005 to authorize NYPA, as
deemed feasible and advisable by its Board of Trustees, to make a
voluntary contribution of $7.5 million to the State to offset losses
to the State from the gross receipts tax revenues from PFJ contract
extensions. This section would also raise the aggregate amount that
NYPA may contribute to the State under the PFJ program from $461.5
million to $469 million.

Section 14 of the bill would amend subdivision 5 of PAL § 1005 to
clarify the purposes for which Niagara and St. Lawrence Project power
may be used.

Section 15 of the bill would repeal subdivision 16 of PAL § 1005 as
added by Chapter 217 of the Laws of 2009. That subdivision has been
implemented and is no longer necessary.

Section 16 of the bill would renumber subdivision 16 of PAL § 1005, as
added by chapter 477 of the Laws of 2009, to be subdivision 17, and
would amend paragraph (a) of such subdivision to authorize NYPA to
offer its energy efficiency programs to ENYPP participants.

Section 17 of the bill contains a severability clause.

Section 18 of the bill contains the effective date.

EXISTING LAW:

The PFJ and ECSB programs providing benefits to eligible applicants
expire June 2, 2010.

Chapter 316 of the Laws of 1997 established the PFJ program to provide
discounted NYPA-purchased power to businesses and not-for-profit
corporations that agree to create or retain jobs in New York State.
In return for such commitments, successful applicants received
three-year contracts for PFJ electricity. The PFJ program originally
made 400 MW of power available and was to be phased in over three
years. As a result of the initial popularity of the program, the PFJ
statute was amended by Chapter 386 of the Laws of 1998 to accelerate
the distribution of the power and increase the size of the program to
450 MW. Chapter 63 of the Laws of 2000 and Chapter 226 of the Laws
of 2002 amended the statute to authorize additional
power to be allocated under the program and to authorize certain
participants to apply for reallocations of power under the program.

Chapter 59 of the Laws of2004 extended program benefits for PFJ
customers whose contracts expired before the end of the PFJ program
in 2005. Such customers were required to choose to receive an
"electricity savings reimbursement" rebate or a power contract
extension.
NYPA was authorized to voluntarily fund the rebates if deemed
feasible and advisable by NYPA's Trustees.

PFJ customers whose contracts expired on or prior to November 30, 2004
were eligible for a rebate to the extent funded by NYPA from the
date their contract expired through December 31, 2005. As an
alternative, these customers could have chosen to receive a rebate to
the extent funded by NYPA from the date their contract expired as a
bridge to a new contract extension, with the contract extension
commencing December 1, 2004. The new contract would be in effect from
a period no earlier than December 1, 2004 through the end of the PFJ
program on December 31, 2005. PFJ customers whose contracts expired
after November 30, 2004 were eligible for rebate or contract
extension from the date their contracts expired through December
31, 2005.

Approved contract extensions entitled customers to receive power from
NYPA pursuant to a sale-for-resale agreement with the customer's
local utility. Separate allocation contracts between customers and
NYPA contained job commitments enforceable by NYPA.

In 2005, provisions of the enacted state budget extended the period
during which PFJ customers could receive benefits until December 31,
2006. Chapter 645 of the Laws of 2006 included provisions extending
program benefits until June 30, 2007. Chapter 89 of the Laws of 2007
included provisions extending program benefits until June 30, 2008.
Chapter 59 of the Laws of 2008 included provisions extending the
program benefits until June 30, 2009. Chapter 217 of the Laws of 2009
included provisions extending program benefits until May 15, 2010.
Chapter 88 of the Laws of 2010 extended program benefits until June
2, 2010.

Chapter 313 of the Laws of 2005 created an ECSB Program. Pursuant to
the ECSB Program, NYPA makes discounted market power available to 94
businesses in the Economic Development Power, High Load Factor Power
and Municipal Distribution Agency Power programs that were facing
price increases before the end of 2006. Up to 70 MW of unallocated
power from the Niagara Power Project and up to 20 MW of currently
unallocated power from the St. Lawrence-FDR Project may be sold into
the market to fund the ECSB Program.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is a new bill.

STATEMENT IN SUPPORT:

The current recession has had a significant impact on New York State
residents and businesses. New York's unemployment rate is at its
highest level in 30 years, reaching 9 percent
in December 2009. From July 2008 to December 2009, New York lost more
than 330,000 jobs, including 73,000 jobs lost in the manufacturing
sector.

Energy cost is a key factor affecting New York State's economic
competitiveness.
Energy intensive businesses currently located within the State and
those considering an expansion or looking to locate in New York need
affordable energy options, Key health care facilities that provide
critical services to their local communities and that employ
thousands of New Yorkers have also been affected by the economic
downturn and rising costs. If affordable energy options do not exist
in New York, many existing businesses and institutions may cease or
curtail operations, and opportunities for new investment in-State
will be lost.

The PFJ and ECSB administered by NYPA are scheduled to expire on June
2, 2010.
Since 1997, these programs have provided low cost power to hundreds of
businesses and institutions statewide, and are among the most
critical job retention programs in New York. The programs currently
support over 300,000 jobs at over 500 businesses and institutions
throughout the State. However, the short-term nature of these
programs, a result of the practice of extending the programs
annually, does not provide sufficient certainty to encourage existing
businesses and institutions to expand or to attract new business
investment in New York, Furthermore, the existing programs are not
supported by dedicated low-cost hydropower resources and the
discounts cannot be continued by NYPA indefinitely in their current
form because NYPA cannot predict with certainty it will have
adequate cash resources to pay for the program.

The new Energize New York Power program would utilize NYPA's unique
and economical hydropower resource to create for the first time a

permanent statewide low-cost power program. The ENYPP would consist
of 455 MW of hydropower and 455 MW of purchased power to create a 910
MW block of below-market rate power that would be used to save
existing jobs in manufacturing, health care, and other industries,
and attract thousands of new jobs and investment to the State.

The hydropower that would be utilized for the ENYPP is currently sold
by NYPA at cost to National Grid, NYSEG, and RG&E to benefit
residential customers under the Rural and Domestic program. The value
of this benefit in 2009 was approximately $82 million, which equated
to an average monthly residential discount of between $2.06 and $4.39
per customer.

Under this bill, residential customers in these utility service
territories would continue to receive a permanent benefit from NYPA.
First, over the first five years after the bill is enacted, NYPA
would transfer funding to National Grid, NYSEG and RG&E to provide
transitional utility bill discounts for residential customers. These
transitional discounts would be funded at $100 million in the first
year, and be reduced by $14 million each year thereafter. Second,
the bill would authorize NYPA to provide $30 million per year in
perpetuity to National Grid, NYSEG and RG&E to provide discounts to
their residential customers. Up to $8 million of this annual
permanent benefit would be set aside for an additional electricity
discount for agricultural consumers taking electric service at the
residential rate.

The Energize New York Power program that would be created by this bill
would protect existing jobs and attract new jobs to the State, and
would encourage new investment to grow the
State's tax base. Eligible businesses and institutions that receive
ENYPP allocations would be allowed to enter up to seven year
contracts, which would provide long-term certainty to encourage new
investment and expansion in New York. The ENYPP would reserve at
least 320 MW for economic development in the National Grid, NYSEG,
and RG&E service territories and 200 MW to attract new investment,
thus ensuring that the bill would result in both job retention and
job creation. In addition, ENYPP would reserve 100 MW for
not-far-profits, such as hospitals, thus protecting jobs in
institutions that provide critical services to our communities.

BUDGET IMPLICATIONS:

This bill would have no impact on the State budget because the
resources for the new ENYPP would be provided by NYPA. Such
resources would consist of hydroelectric power and other resources
deemed feasible and advisable by the NYPA Trustees.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This bill would take effect immediately and be deemed to be in full
force and effect on and after May 15, 2010; provided that sections 9,

10 and 11 of the bill would take effect on the same date and in the
same manner as Chapter 88 of the Laws of 2010. The amendments to the
provisions of law relating to the PFJ and ECSB programs would not
effect the expiration of such provisions of law and would be deemed
repealed with them.

summary: Creates the Energize New York power program; extends the expiration of the power for jobs program and the energy cost savings benefit program; authorizes certain contributions to the state general fund.
